title: Methods in Context: Theoretical & Practical Issues
welcome_lead: Positivists count, interpretivists listen — and budgets always bite.

walkthroughs.body_html: Comte (1842) founded positivism: social facts can be measured. Prefers quantitative methods — surveys, statistics. Weber argued for verstehen — empathetic understanding. Interpretivists prefer qualitative — interviews, ethnography. Most modern sociology mixes both.

Funding, time and access shape research. ESRC grants average £200k for a multi-year project. Funder bias: corporate funders may steer findings. Researchers' own characteristics matter — male researchers struggle to do feminist research; outsiders may miss subcultural meanings.

Random sampling: every member equal chance. Stratified: divided by characteristic. Snowball: through referrals. Opportunity: convenience. Small samples undermine generalisability. Pre-registration and peer review provide some quality control.

Which sampling method works best for hard-to-reach hidden populations?
Why do positivists and interpretivists prefer different methods?
options: Positivists like numbers and interpretivists like words — that's the whole difference.
Both positivists and interpretivists prefer experiments above all else.

Positivists treat sociology like natural science, seeking objective measurable patterns — preferring quantitative methods. Interpretivists believe humans construct meaning, requiring qualitative methods to access subjective experience.
